claim: `query_relay_all` loops fetching 500-event pages until the relay returns a short page. There is no page-count cap, no total-event cap, and no check that the cursor actually advanced. `get_channels` calls it twice, once at line 147 with a filter that has no author, no `#p`, and no time bound at all (`{"kinds": [39000]}`), so the loop accumulates every channel-metadata event the relay is willing to serve into a single in-memory `Vec`. Since `query_relay` never verifies signatures (relay.rs:315-341 -> parse_json_response at relay.rs:206-231 deserializes without calling `verify()`), the relay fully controls both page contents and page length.
failure_scenario: The renderer calls `get_channels` (channels.rs:79 — invoked on every app load and channel-list refresh). A hostile or compromised relay answers each `POST /query` with exactly 500 synthetic kind:39000 events and ignores the `until`/`before_id` cursor that `advance_directory_cursor` (channels.rs:35-40) writes back into the filter. Because `done` is only ever true when `page.len() < DIRECTORY_PAGE_SIZE`, the loop at channels.rs:53-64 never terminates: `all.extend(page)` grows unboundedly until the desktop process is OOM-killed. Even a merely large honest relay makes this an unbounded client-side download, since the line-147 filter selects every kind:39000 on the relay rather than the user's channels.

claim: reader_authorized_for_event() fails open for the two cleartext, relay-signed, globally-stored P_GATED kinds it does NOT name - member-added (44100) and member-removed (44101) notifications - so the kindless {ids:[X]} read path leaks private channel-membership metadata despite the #p read-gate. Confirms and narrows the breadth pass filter.rs:23 item: caller event_visible_to_reader (buzz-relay handlers/req.rs:1245) relies on this function as its sole per-event backstop, and p_gated_filters_authorized (req.rs:1077) deliberately exempts kindless ids lookups for every kind except KIND_DM_VISIBILITY/KIND_AGENT_TURN_METRIC. Root cause: RESULT_GATED_KINDS (kind.rs:129), hardcoded here, is a strict subset of P_GATED_KINDS (kind.rs:146).
failure_scenario: An authenticated community member who learns the 32-byte event id of a kind:44100/44101 notification sends REQ {ids:[<id>]}. p_gated_filters_authorized returns true (ids exemption, kind not named). Historical delivery calls event_visible_to_reader -> reader_authorized_for_event; because kind==44100 is neither KIND_DM_VISIBILITY nor KIND_AGENT_TURN_METRIC, line 25 returns true. The relay delivers the cleartext event built at side_effects.rs:934 (content type=member_added, channel_id uuid, actor hex; p-tag=target; h-tag=channel uuid), revealing that pubkey P was added/removed from a possibly-private channel C by actor A, to a reader who is not the #p target.

claim: getThreadReference picks the FIRST `e` tag marked "root" (`eventTags.find(...)`) but the LAST `e` tag marked "reply" (line 37, `[...eventTags].reverse().find(...)`). The relay's resolve_nip10_thread_meta (crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs:595-607) assigns `root_hex` and `reply_hex` in a forward loop that overwrites on every match, so BOTH end up as the last-marked tag, and the ancestry check at ingest.rs:672-674 / 700-702 (`if client_root_bytes != parent_root { return Err("root tag does not match thread ancestry") }`) validates only that last root tag. The two sides therefore agree on `reply` but disagree on `root`, so a reply can carry a truthful trailing root tag that satisfies the relay and a forged leading root tag that the desktop uses for thread grouping.
failure_scenario: Mallory posts a reply in #general with tags `[["h", channelId], ["e", VICTIM_THREAD_ROOT_ID, "", "root"], ["e", REAL_ROOT_ID, "", "root"], ["e", REAL_PARENT_ID, "", "reply"]]`. The relay's loop at ingest.rs:595-607 keeps the last root (REAL_ROOT_ID) and the last reply (REAL_PARENT_ID), so `client_root_bytes == parent_root` and the event is accepted and indexed under the real thread. Every desktop client then calls getThreadReference, which returns `rootId = VICTIM_THREAD_ROOT_ID` (first root tag) with `parentId = REAL_PARENT_ID`. Because subtree membership and unread tallies are keyed on `rootId` (features/channels/lib/threadBadgeCounts.ts:11-16 states "Subtree membership is keyed on each reply's rootId") and the read-state contexts are `thread:<rootId>` (features/channels/readState/readStateManager.ts THREAD_PREFIX), the reply is counted into — and, in thread views built from rootId, displayed inside — a thread it does not belong to. Pointing the first root tag at a non-existent 64-hex id instead makes the reply's thread context unreachable and drives useLoadMissingAncestors to issue relay fetches for an id that will never resolve.
evidence: const rootTag = eventTags.find((tag) => tag[3] === "root");
reported_slice: desktop-messages (deep pass, Lens B — cryptography, keys, identity)

claim: The kindless-`ids` read exemption is only revoked for the two kinds in `RESULT_GATED_KINDS`, but `P_GATED_KINDS` (buzz-core/src/kind.rs:146) lists six. A kindless `{ids:[…]}` REQ therefore passes both the filter-layer `#p` gate here AND the per-event gate (`reader_authorized_for_event`, buzz-core/src/filter.rs:25, which returns `true` for every kind except 30622 and 44200), so kinds 44100, 44101 and 1059 are delivered to any authenticated reader who knows the event id — even though the comment directly above this line says the exemption is 'only safe for kinds whose id is author-bound or whose content is encrypted'.
failure_scenario: Member M of a community learns the 32-byte id of a kind:44100 member-added notification addressed to another user V (e.g. from an earlier session in which M was still a member of that channel, from a log, or from a client cache). M authenticates and sends `["REQ","x",{"ids":["<id>"]}]`. At req.rs:1054 `filter.kinds` is None so `can_match_p_gated` is true; at req.rs:1071 `explicitly_no_ids_exemption` is false because `kinds` is absent, so line 1077 returns `true` and the filter-layer gate is skipped. Historical delivery then calls `event_visible_to_reader` (req.rs:1237), which passes: 44100 is not in AUTHOR_ONLY_KINDS, not shared-gated, and `reader_authorized_for_event` short-circuits to `true` at filter.rs:25 because the kind is neither 30622 nor 44200. The channel-membership filter no-ops because these events are stored with `channel_id = None` (side_effects.rs:939-942). M receives the event, whose content is plaintext JSON `{"type":"member_added","channel_id":"…","actor":"…"}` plus the `p` tag naming V and the `h` tag naming the channel — i.e. who was added to which private channel and by whom. Kind 1059 gift wraps leak recipient/timing metadata by the same path.

claim: The Redis cross-pod live fan-out path applies only `filter_fanout_by_access`, which gates AUTHOR_ONLY_KINDS (line 139) and SHARED_GATED_KINDS (line 157) and channel visibility — but never the viewer-private owner check for RESULT_GATED_KINDS. That check exists only as inline code in the local ingest path (`dispatch_persistent_event`, lines 461-491). So the same kind:30622 / kind:44200 event is owner-gated when fanned out by the pod that ingested it and un-gated when fanned out by every other pod, contradicting the doc on `reader_authorized_for_event` (buzz-core/src/filter.rs:19-22) that claims it guards 'live fan-out (`event.rs`)'.
failure_scenario: In a multi-pod deployment, pod A ingests a kind:44200 agent turn metric addressed to owner V and publishes it to Redis. Pod B receives it and calls `fan_out_pubsub_event` (event.rs:282), which builds a StoredEvent and reaches line 307. An attacker connected to pod B holding a subscription whose filter matched the p-gate exemption at req.rs:1077 (kindless plus known `ids`) gets a match from `fan_out_scoped`; `filter_fanout_by_access` does not strip them because 44200 is in neither AUTHOR_ONLY_KINDS nor SHARED_GATED_KINDS and the event is global (`channel_id = None`, so the function returns at line 178 before the channel checks). The frame is sent. Had the identical event been fanned out on pod A, the `private_event_owner` filter at lines 477-491 would have dropped that recipient. The precondition is the same id-knowledge requirement as the REQ path, so this is a defense-in-depth divergence rather than an unauthenticated leak, but it means the two live-delivery surfaces enforce different policies for the same event.
evidence: let matches = filter_fanout_by_access(state, community_id, &stored, matches, None).await;

claim: `parseNostrpairUri` accepts relay URLs from a scanned QR code after checking only that the scheme is `ws` or `wss` — no host validation whatsoever. The codebase already has a hardened validator for exactly this (`validateInviteRelayUri` in mobile/lib/shared/relay/relay_validation.dart, which rejects non-WSS outside debug, loopback, RFC1918, CGNAT, link-local, IPv4 literals in decimal/hex/leading-zero form, and non-global IPv6) and the invite deep-link path calls it (deep_link.dart line 170). The pairing QR path never does: `_pairNipAb` takes `qr.relays.first` (pairing_provider.dart line 178) and hands it straight to `PairingSocket`, which does `WebSocketChannel.connect(Uri.parse(_wsUrl))` (pairing_socket.dart line 63).
failure_scenario: An attacker prints or displays a QR encoding `nostrpair://<64-hex pubkey>?secret=<64-hex>&relay=ws%3A%2F%2F192.168.1.1%3A8080&v=1`. The user scans it on the pairing screen; pairing_page.dart line 54 passes the raw scanned string to `pair()`, which routes to `_pairNipAb`. The app opens a plaintext WebSocket to the victim's LAN gateway (or `ws://127.0.0.1:<port>` against another app on the device), sends a NIP-42 AUTH event signed with an ephemeral key, then a kind:24134 offer — turning the phone into an unauthenticated request source inside its own network segment, and doing the whole pairing handshake in cleartext where a local network attacker can read the session traffic. The SAS code still protects the key transfer itself, but the connection/probe happens before any user confirmation.

claim: The open-channel live subscription filters with since = local wall-clock now with zero skew allowance, so any incoming message whose sender-signed created_at is even one second behind the local clock is excluded by the relay's filter and never delivered live; with a fast local clock, live delivery for the open channel silently fails entirely.
failure_scenario: _init() (line 74) subscribes with since: _currentUnixSeconds() (line 88, local DateTime.now()), then fetches history. A peer whose device clock is 30s behind (common on Android without NTT sync) sends a message: its created_at is 30s older than the mobile client's since bound, the relay's NIP-01 filter check rejects it for this subscription, and the earlier history fetch already completed - the message appears only after the user leaves and re-enters the channel. The codebase itself acknowledges skew elsewhere (relay_session's _reconnectReplaySkewSeconds = 5, and channels_provider's list subscription uses limit:0 with no since), making this filter the odd one out. channel_window.dart line 333 additionally drops live rows older than the loaded window bottom, so even a since fix needs care.
evidence: since: _currentUnixSeconds(),

claim: _publish silently drops a scheduled publish when another publish is in flight (if (_isPublishing) return;) without rescheduling, and dispose() only flushes when a debounce timer is still pending, so read-state advances made during a slow in-flight publish are never synced to the relay until some unrelated later markContextRead.

User reads channel A (publish starts), then reads channel B; the 5s debounce fires during the in-flight publish, _publish() returns immediately at line 388 with the timer already consumed (_debounceTimer = null in _schedulePublish's callback, line 376). Both requests reach Db::open_dm (lib.rs:2609) -> dm::open_dm (dm.rs:378, fast-path SELECT finds nothing) -> create_dm; both transactions pass the in-tx SELECT at dm.rs:131-150, both INSERT at dm.rs:166-179 with the same (community_id, participant_hash). claim: The community custom-emoji palette resolves shortcode collisions purely by comparing attacker-chosen `event.created_at` values with no upper bound, so any member can publish a kind:30030 set with a far-future timestamp and permanently take over every shortcode in the community — no honest member can ever outbid the forged timestamp.
failure_scenario: Attacker path: (1) A community member publishes their own kind:30030 emoji set (relay ingest explicitly allowlists member-authored 30030 — see the module doc at customEmoji.ts:12-14 and crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs:413) containing `["emoji", "thumbsup", "https://attacker.example/beacon.png"]` for every shortcode already in use in the community, and sets `created_at = 4102444800`. The relay does not bound future `created_at` on ingest and performs no validation of the emoji tag's URL. (2) Every client calls `listCustomEmoji()` → `fetchCommunityEmojiEvents()` (customEmoji.ts:137-146, `limit: 500` across all members) → `unionCustomEmoji(events)`. (3) unionCustomEmoji at customEmoji.ts:122-128 picks the winner with `event.created_at > winner.createdAt`, so the year-2100 set wins every shortcode. (4) The winning URL flows into `remarkCustomEmoji`, which stamps it onto the node at remarkCustomEmoji.ts:145 as `hProperties.src`, and is rendered as an `` in every message that uses that shortcode. Because Math-style timestamp comparison is the only tiebreak and there is no clamp against `Date.now()`, the hijack is permanent for the life of the community: a legitimate re-publish would need a still-larger timestamp. Impact: community-wide emoji substitution (content spoofing) plus an unrevokable per-render beacon to an attacker-controlled host that leaks each viewer's IP and User-Agent.

claim: The anti-phishing masked-link check fails open: any href whose scheme is not http/https makes `isMaskedLink` return `false` ("not masked"), so the destination-revealing tooltip is suppressed exactly for the schemes that are least obvious to the reader — and `defaultUrlTransform` lets `mailto:`, `xmpp:`, `irc:` and `ircs:` through to both the anchor and the OS opener.

(2) nodeCache.ts:108 runs the href through `messageLinkUrlTransform` (ui/markdown/utils.ts:174-179), which delegates to react-markdown's `defaultUrlTransform`; its safe-protocol regex is `^(https?|ircs?|mailto|xmpp)$`, so `mailto:` survives unchanged. (3) markdown.tsx:1471-1479 renders it via `ExternalLinkAnchor`, which wraps the anchor in `MaskedLinkTooltip` (markdown.tsx:1323). (4) MaskedLinkTooltip.tsx:27 calls `isMaskedLink(label, href)`. (5) maskedLink.ts:17-18 does `const hrefUrl = parseExternal(href); if (!hrefUrl) return false;` — `parseExternal` (maskedLink.ts:42-58) returns `null` for anything not matching `^https?://`, so the function reports "not masked" and the tooltip is skipped entirely. The reader sees link text that reads as a GitHub URL, with no hover reveal of the real destination — the precise scenario the module docstring (maskedLink.ts:1-12) says this control exists to prevent. (6) Left-click renders a plain `<a href="mailto:..." target="_blank">` (markdown.tsx:1308-1315) and the right-click "Open link" item calls `openUrl(href)` (markdown.tsx:1334), handing the attacker-chosen non-http URL to the OS handler. The bug is that the guard's failure mode is 'no warning' rather than 'always warn' — a non-http href should be treated as maximally masked, not as unmasked.

claim: History subscriptions accumulate every relay-supplied EVENT frame into an unbounded in-memory array; the `limit` the client puts in its REQ filter is never enforced on the receiving side, so a hostile or compromised relay can stream events until the renderer runs out of memory within the 25-second history timeout.
failure_scenario: Attacker path: a relay the user has joined (observer relays are opened against arbitrary user-supplied URLs — see `withReadOnlyRelayClient(relayUrl, ...)` at readOnlyRelayClient.ts:320-330, and the primary relay is equally untrusted under Nostr's model) answers any REQ by streaming EVENT frames indefinitely and never sending EOSE. (1) `handleWsMessage` parses each frame at readOnlyRelayClient.ts:227 and, at readOnlyRelayClient.ts:238-240, pushes `rest[1] as RelayEvent` onto `histories.get(subId).events` with no count check, no size check, and no validation that the object is even shaped like an event. (2) The only bound is the `HISTORY_TIMEOUT_MS = 25_000` timer (relayClientTimings.ts:10) armed at readOnlyRelayClient.ts:172-176; nothing caps the array in the meantime, and the requested `filter.limit` (readOnlyRelayClient.ts:180) is never re-checked. (3) The identical pattern exists on the primary relay client: relayClosedRecovery.ts:132-134 `if (subscription.mode === "history") { subscription.events.push(event); return false; }`, reached from relayClientSession.ts:783-786 and :859. A relay pushing multi-kilobyte events at line rate for 25s accumulates hundreds of megabytes of retained JS objects (each `push` also keeps the parsed tag arrays alive), crashing or hard-freezing the webview. Requesting `limit: 10_000` (relayChannelFilters.ts:143) without enforcing it client-side is the gap between 'we asked for a bound' and 'we act on the bound'.
evidence: this.histories.get(rest[0])?.events.push(rest[1] as RelayEvent);

claim: count_events_on silently ignores EventQuery::shared_gated_reader. The SELECT builder query_events_on applies the shared-gate visibility clause at event.rs:538-550 (`AND (kind NOT IN (SHARED_GATED_KINDS) OR pubkey = $reader OR tags @> '[["shared","true"]]')`), but the COUNT builder ends at line 764 without ever reading that field — even though callers set it on the very struct they hand to the count path (buzz-relay/src/handlers/count.rs:163 and :235, buzz-relay/src/api/bridge.rs:1547). The only thing preventing a private-event count leak is a separate `&& !needs_shared_gate_filtering` term in the caller's if-condition; the field itself is a no-op, which is exactly the shape the route_proof module warns about at lib.rs:330 ("if the two ever drift ... the routed COUNT seam is unsound").
failure_scenario: A reader issues a NIP-45 COUNT for a shared-gated kind (SHARED_GATED_KINDS, e.g. 30175/30178) authored by another user. count.rs:163 sets query.shared_gated_reader = Some(reader) and the code today falls into the query+post-filter branch only because of the extra `!needs_shared_gate_filtering` guard on the same condition. If that guard is dropped, reordered, or a new caller (or the bridge's future count seam) constructs the same EventQuery and calls count_events/count_events_routed directly, count_events_on emits SQL with no visibility predicate and returns the count of other users' non-shared private events. Combined with attacker-chosen `authors`, `since`, and `until` on the same filter, the counts binary-search the existence and timing of private items the SELECT path would never return.

claim: When a historical-delivery DB query fails mid-REQ, the handler sends EOSE — the NIP-01 "end of stored events" success signal — and returns, silently truncating history instead of reporting the error. Every other error branch in the same function correctly sends CLOSED.
failure_scenario: A client subscribes with two filters, e.g. `["REQ","s",{"#h":"<ch>","kinds":[9],"limit":500},{"#h":"<ch>","kinds":[7]}]`. `query_events_routed` for filter 0 fails (Postgres pool exhaustion, statement timeout, connection reset). The loop at req.rs:320 hits the Err arm, logs a warn, sends EOSE for the subscription and returns — filter 1 is never executed and the already-delivered events from filter 0 (possibly zero) are all the client gets. The client receives a well-formed EOSE and concludes it has the complete stored history, so the UI renders an empty or partial channel with no error and no retry. Compare req.rs:100, :154 and :100's sibling paths, which send `RelayMessage::closed(&sub_id, "error: database error")` for the same class of failure.

claim: A single transient full send buffer during historical delivery aborts the REQ without ever sending EOSE, while the connection stays open and the subscription stays registered — the client waits for an EOSE that will never arrive.
failure_scenario: `conn.send` returns false on the first buffer-full (connection.rs:88-105) but only cancels the connection after `grace_limit` consecutive fulls (default 15, config.rs:519-522). A client on a slow link issues a broad REQ; the relay pushes historical events faster than the socket drains, the 1000-slot data channel (config.rs:508-511, BUZZ_SEND_BUFFER default 1000) fills once, `conn.send` returns false, and `handle_req` returns at req.rs:399 — skipping the `conn.send(RelayMessage::eose(&sub_id))` at req.rs:408. The counter is reset by the next successful send (connection.rs:92), so the socket is not closed and live fan-out for that subscription continues. Most Nostr clients block their "loading history" state until EOSE, so the channel view spins indefinitely even though new events keep arriving. The NIP-50 search lane has the identical shape at req.rs:726-727 returning before the EOSE at req.rs:739.

claim: For kind:9007 (NIP-29 create-group) the channel row is created in the DB at ingest.rs:2497 before imeta validation runs at ingest.rs:2605-2613. An imeta rejection returns an error without running the `pre_created_channel` compensation, which only exists on the event-insert failure path (ingest.rs:2801), leaving an orphaned channel row and a permanently un-retryable create.
failure_scenario: A client (or attacker) submits a signed kind:9007 with `["h","<client-chosen-uuid>"]`, a valid `name` tag, and an `imeta` tag whose `url` points at a blob that does not exist in this tenant's media store. Flow: `create_channel_with_id` succeeds (ingest.rs:2497-2510), `pre_created_channel = Some(client_uuid)` (ingest.rs:2519). kind:9007 is not in `requires_h_channel_scope` (ingest.rs:477-506) so no thread-metadata step intervenes, and it is not kind 0 or 7, so the next reachable failure point is `verify_imeta_blobs` at ingest.rs:2610, which returns `IngestError::Rejected` via `?`. That `?` returns straight out of `ingest_event_inner` — it never reaches the `match ... Err(e) =>` block at ingest.rs:2798 where `soft_delete_channel(tenant.community(), ch_id)` is the compensation. The user sees `OK false "invalid: ..."` ("channel creation failed") but the channel row exists and lists them as owner. Resending the same event returns `accepted: false, "duplicate: channel already exists"` (ingest.rs:2512-2518) forever, so the client's natural retry can never succeed, and each distinct crafted UUID mints another orphan channel row that no event references.

claim: The HTTP NIP-98 event-submission path builds its IngestAuth with Scope::all_known() — which includes AdminChannels and AdminUsers — so the ingest scope check for admin-gated kinds is always satisfied for any NIP-98-authenticated relay member submitting over HTTP POST /events. This is a second, independently-reachable instance of the over-grant the breadth pass attributed only to verify_auth_event (NIP-42/WebSocket); the HTTP path never calls verify_auth_event and hard-codes the full scope set here.
failure_scenario: An attacker who is a relay member (or passes NIP-OA membership) signs a kind:9030/9031/9032 (RELAY_ADMIN_ADD_MEMBER/REMOVE_MEMBER/CHANGE_ROLE) or kind:9000/9001/9005 NIP-29 admin event and POSTs it to /events with a valid NIP-98 Authorization header. In submit_event_authed the auth is built as IngestAuth::Http { scopes: Scope::all_known() }. In ingest.rs, required_scope_for_kind returns Scope::AdminChannels/AdminUsers (line 260/269) and the gate `if !auth.scopes().contains(&required)` (line 1904) passes because all_known() contains both admin scopes. claim: On reconnect the per-subscription replay window's since is derived from lastSeenCreatedAt (the max created_at seen on the live subscription); created_at is sender-chosen (only bounded by the relay's plus/minus 15-minute drift check, and honest clock skew of even a minute exceeds the 5-second RECONNECT_REPLAY_SKEW_SECS tolerance), so a future-dated message pushes since past real time and messages that arrive during a disconnect are never replayed and silently missing.
failure_scenario: A member posts a message with created_at ~10 minutes in the future (accepted: within plus/minus 15-min drift, ingest.rs:1862). Every viewer's live subscription runs prepareSubscriptionEvent (relayClosedRecovery.ts:141) setting lastSeenCreatedAt to that future value. Their socket drops (VPN blip/sleep). On reconnect replaySince = lastSeenCreatedAt - 5s (~10 min future) and buildReconnectReplayFilter sets REQ since to it (relayReconnectReplay.ts:61); the relay returns nothing older than that instant, so real messages posted during the outage (timestamps ~now) fall below since and never arrive — the timeline is missing messages with no error shown.

claim: read_sidecar_mime collapses every get_sidecar failure — transient S3 5xx/timeout/connection reset and malformed sidecar JSON alike — into None via `.ok()`, with no tracing call anywhere in the function. Entry: GET /media/{sha}.{ext} -> buzz-relay/src/api/media.rs:604 get_blob -> media.rs:619 serve_blob_for_tenant -> media.rs:642 read_sidecar_mime -> storage.rs:231. The S3 error becomes None, which becomes `.ok_or(MediaError::NotFound)?` at media.rs:644 -> HTTP 404. The client's image renders as permanently broken rather than retryable, and because the same collapse also swallows serde_json failures (storage.rs:203) a single truncated sidecar object makes that blob 404 forever with zero log lines from the media crate to point an operator at it. claim: The 3840x2160 resolution cap reads `track.width()`/`track.height()`, which in mp4-0.14.0 (src/track.rs:150-163) return the `avc1` VisualSampleEntry's declared u16 width/height fields — a container annotation. The real coded frame size lives in the H.264 SPS inside `avcC`, which mp4-0.14.0 stores as raw `NalUnit` bytes (src/mp4box/avc1.rs:168) and which buzz-media never parses. Every decoder allocates from the SPS, not from avc1. The check therefore constrains a number nobody uses.
failure_scenario: Attacker uploads an MP4 whose `avc1` box declares width=320, height=240 while the SPS in `avcC` declares 16384x16384. validation.rs:289 `validate_video_file` runs check_moov_before_mdat, validate_mp4_metadata_free (avc1/avcC live under the allowlisted stsd, so the box-allowlist passes), then reads track.width()=320 and track.height()=240 at lines 362-363 and lets it through. The blob is stored verbatim (upload.rs:466 `storage.put_file`) and the sidecar records `dim = "320x240"` (upload.rs:471), which is what BlobDescriptor.dim reports to clients. Any mobile/desktop client that trusts that dim to size a player and then hands the stream to its H.264 decoder allocates from the SPS instead — a client-side decode bomb the relay's ResolutionTooHigh gate was written to prevent. Same for the reverse direction: a legitimate 4K clip can be rejected or accepted purely on an attacker-chosen container field.

claim: The blob is PUT to S3 before metadata generation, and the comment justifies the resulting orphans as negligible because blobs are "content-addressed". Content-addressing only deduplicates identical bytes; every distinct crafted payload yields a distinct sha256 and therefore a distinct permanent object. There is no GC (the code says a sweeper is a future V2 job), and the failure path is trivially attacker-triggerable: a payload that passes the cheap structural validators but fails `image::load_from_memory` leaves a full-size orphan with no sidecar and no `_uploads/` moderation record.
failure_scenario: Attacker builds a 50 MB PNG: valid 8-byte signature, a small IHDR declaring e.g. 100x100, one `IDAT` chunk holding 50 MB of random bytes with a correctly computed CRC, then IEND. validate_png_metadata_free (validation.rs:592) accepts it — IDAT is critical so the ancillary gate at line 644 is skipped and no CRC or zlib check is performed — and imagesize reports 100x100, under the 25 MP cap. process_buffered_upload then executes `storage.put(&key, &body, &mime)` at upload.rs:141, writing 50 MB durably. Only afterwards does prepare_metadata run generate_image_metadata_sync (thumbnail.rs:26), where zlib rejects the IDAT and the whole upload returns MediaError::InvalidImage — logged at upload.rs:154 as "orphan blob left for GC" that never comes. Because no sidecar is written the object is unreachable and uncountable per-community (bucket_index classifies it only as orphan_blob_bytes), and because record_upload_event runs after prepare_metadata (upload.rs:162) no moderation record exists either. At the default 30 uploads/minute/pubkey (crates/buzz-relay/src/config.rs:740) each key can durably write ~1.5 GB/minute of unbilled, unreferenced, never-collected S3 objects while every request returns an error the operator reads as "rejected, cost nothing".

claim: The JPEG APP0 exemption is documented as accepting only canonical JFIF headers whose "lengths and identifiers are fixed", but the accepted length is parameterised by the attacker-chosen thumbnail dimensions `payload[12]` (Xthumbnail) and `payload[13]` (Ythumbnail). Any payload of exactly `14 + 3*X*Y` bytes starting with `JFIF\0` is blessed, so the trailing `3*X*Y` bytes are arbitrary attacker data. The 16-bit segment length caps one segment at ~65 KB, but nothing limits the number of APP0 segments, so the channel scales to the whole 50 MB image cap. The 7 bytes of version/units/Xdensity/Ydensity are likewise unconstrained — the same identity channel the PNG validator explicitly excludes pHYs for.
failure_scenario: A malicious or backdoored client (or anyone with an accepted Blossom key) emits a JPEG containing `FF E0` with length 0xFF12, payload `JFIF\0` + version/units/density + Xthumbnail=147, Ythumbnail=148, followed by 65268 bytes of GPS coordinates, a device fingerprint, or an encrypted beacon; repeat the segment N times. validate_jpeg_metadata_free (validation.rs:502) computes canonical_jfif = true at lines 554-556 for each segment and passes, so validate_content returns image/jpeg. zune-jpeg-0.5.15 src/decoder.rs:571-589 reads APP(0), sniffs only the first 5 bytes for `AVI1\0`, and skips the rest, so `image::load_from_memory` in thumbnail.rs:26 decodes normally and a thumbnail/blurhash are produced. upload.rs:141 stores the body byte-for-byte and the relay serves it back at GET /media/{sha}.jpg. The module's stated guarantee — a structural allowlist because "location can also live in XMP, comments, PNG text, ICC descriptions, or private chunks" — is defeated for the most common upload format, and there is no test covering it (the only APP0 negative test, validation.rs:1383, uses a 6-byte payload that fails the len>=14 precondition).

claim: The generic-file path takes its canonical extension straight from infer's table when file_mime_to_ext has no mapping, and infer 0.19 emits exactly one uppercase extension: `application/x-compress` -> "Z" (verified in infer-0.19.0/src/map.rs:555-560). Every serve-side gate is lowercase-only — is_safe_ext in crates/buzz-relay/src/api/media.rs:534 accepts only 'a'..='z' | '0'..='9' — so a `.Z` upload is accepted, billed, blob-stored, sidecar-published and moderation-recorded, but is unreachable through every read path. The authors already knew about this infer quirk: bucket_index.rs:82-85 was widened to mixed-case specifically so `{sha}.Z` classifies as a Blob, but the corresponding widening was never applied to the serve path. That mismatch is what makes the dead bytes invisible: because the sweep sees both the blob and its sidecar binding, finish() (bucket_index.rs:294-297) does not count them as orphan_blob bytes, so no gauge ever reports the leak.
failure_scenario: A user attaches a Unix compress archive (magic 0x1f 0x9d, e.g. an old `foo.tar.Z`) via PUT /upload. validate_file_content returns ("application/x-compress", "Z"); the blob is written at key `{sha}.Z` and the sidecar records ext="Z". build_descriptor (upload.rs:550) produces url `.../{sha}.Z`, then rewrite_descriptor_urls_for_tenant (crates/buzz-relay/src/api/media.rs:464-470) runs is_safe_ext("Z") -> false and silently rewrites the URL to `.../{sha}.bin`. The client gets HTTP 200 and a URL. Fetching it: serve_blob_for_tenant compares requested_ext "bin" against sidecar.ext "Z" (crates/buzz-relay/src/api/media.rs:652-654) -> 404. Fetching the bare hash instead is no better: resolve_s3_key rejects the sidecar's own ext via is_safe_ext (crates/buzz-relay/src/api/media.rs:877-879) -> 404. The file is therefore permanently unreachable by any URL while consuming storage forever, and the orphan sweep will never flag it because it has a valid sidecar binding.

claim: In `handle_ephemeral_event`'s kind:20001 presence branch, the 128-byte length cap is applied only on the bare-string branch (`else if raw.len() > 128`). The JSON branch — taken whenever the content starts with `{` — ends in `.unwrap_or(raw)`, which hands back the *entire untruncated* content when the JSON fails to parse or has no string `status` field, and returns an unbounded `status` string when it does parse. The resulting value is written verbatim into Redis by `set_presence` (event.rs:819-822 → buzz-pubsub/src/presence.rs:36-42, a plain `SET key status EX ttl` with no length check). Ephemeral events never reach `ingest_event_inner`'s 256 KB content cap (handlers/ingest.rs:1868-1875) because `handle_event` dispatches them at event.rs:698-719 before ingest, so the only bound on `raw` is the 512 KB WebSocket frame limit (config.rs:14, `DEFAULT_MAX_FRAME_BYTES: usize = 512 * 1024`).
failure_scenario: An authenticated member sends a signed kind:20001 event whose content is `{` followed by ~500 KB of non-JSON filler. `serde_json::from_str` fails, `.ok()` yields `None`, `.and_then(...)` yields `None`, and `.unwrap_or(raw)` returns the full ~500 KB string. `set_presence` stores that as the value of `presence:<community>:<pubkey>`. Repeating from N distinct member keys, or from one key on a loop, inflates Redis memory by ~500 KB per key and makes every `get_presence_bulk` fan-out (used by the bridge's `synthesize_presence`, bridge.rs:1978) return megabytes to every client that asks for a member roster — amplifying one 512 KB frame into unbounded egress. The 128-byte cap the author clearly intended is simply not on the reachable path.

claim: `enforce_ws_admission` reads the connection's auth state and returns `true` (admit, no counter incremented) for every connection that is not yet Authenticated. All WebSocket rate limiting — LimitType::WsEvents and LimitType::Messages — is therefore keyed on the authenticated pubkey and applies only after NIP-42 auth succeeds; an unauthenticated socket is subject to no per-message quota at all, only the process-global `handler_semaphore` (connection.rs:511, 541, 559) and the process-global `conn_semaphore` (state.rs:727).
failure_scenario: An unauthenticated peer opens a WebSocket, never sends AUTH, and floods EVENT/REQ/COUNT frames for the full 5-second window before AUTH_TIMEOUT (connection.rs:27) cancels it. Each EVENT reaches handlers::event::handle_event and each REQ reaches handlers::req::handle_req after `enforce_ws_admission` waves it through at line 608. Because the only backstop is a shared global semaphore, the flood competes directly with authenticated traffic for handler permits; N such sockets opened in a loop exhaust `handler_semaphore` and every legitimate client starts receiving 'rate-limited: too many concurrent requests'. Nothing charges the abuser a quota, and nothing keyed on the abuser's IP exists (see the companion finding on `check_ip_connection`).

AuthState::Authenticated(ctx) => (ctx.pubkey, ctx.agent_owner_pubkey.is_some()),
            _ => return true,
reported_slice: auth (crates/buzz-auth, crates/buzz-acp) + the call sites where their auth decisions are made or re-made

claim: The git HTTP routes are the only NIP-98-authenticated surface in the relay that never marks the token in the shared replay seen-set. Every other NIP-98 route calls `bridge::check_nip98_replay` (bridge.rs:770, 960, 1401, 2092; invites.rs:258) or `try_mark_in_scope` (operator.rs:111); the git path calls `verify_nip98_event` at line 188 and then explicitly opts out. Combined with the deliberately tautological method check (event_method is read from the event's own tags at lines 168-176) and with `git_expected_url` (lines 236-253) stripping `/info/refs`, `/git-upload-pack` and `/git-receive-pack` down to the bare repo root, one captured Authorization header is a bearer credential valid for every git verb on that repository for the whole ±60s window, unlimited times.
failure_scenario: A deployment where `config.relay_url` does not start with `wss://` serves git over plaintext http (git_expected_url line 241-245 selects the `http` scheme in that case). An on-path observer, a logging reverse proxy, or any component that records request headers captures one `Authorization: Nostr <base64>` token from a developer's `git clone`. Within the next 60 seconds the attacker replays the identical header against `POST /git/{owner}/{repo}/git-receive-pack` on the same host: the `u` tag still matches because both endpoints normalise to the repo root, the method check compares the event's own `method` tag against itself and cannot fail, and no seen-set consult happens because the code at line 194 declines to do one. The relay accepts the request as the victim's pubkey and runs the push through `enforce_relay_membership` and the pre-receive hook under the victim's identity.

claim: Every outbound JSON-RPC request is serialized in full and written to a tracing event at debug level before it is sent. The `session/new` request built at acp.rs:629-646 carries `mcpServers`, and `build_mcp_servers` (lib.rs:4179-4207) places the agent's Nostr secret key into that structure verbatim as `EnvVar { name: "BUZZ_PRIVATE_KEY", value: config.keys.secret_key().to_bech32() }` (lib.rs:4198-4205). The harness installs an EnvFilter from `RUST_LOG` at lib.rs:1276, so turning on debug logging — the normal first step when diagnosing an agent — writes the full `nsec1...` into the log stream. `hide_env_values = true` on the clap arg (config.rs:243) and the best-effort zeroize of the CLI string (config.rs:840-842) show the authors intended the key never to be printed; this path defeats both.
failure_scenario: An operator runs the harness with `RUST_LOG=debug` (or `buzz_acp=debug`) to diagnose an agent that is not responding. On the next session creation, acp.rs:1074 emits `→ {"jsonrpc":"2.0",...,"mcpServers":[{..."env":[{"name":"BUZZ_PRIVATE_KEY","value":"nsec1..."}]}]}`. That line lands in whatever the harness's stderr is attached to — a systemd journal, a container log shipper, a desktop log file, a pasted bug report. Anyone with read access to those logs recovers the agent's signing key and can thereafter sign arbitrary Nostr events as that agent, authenticate to the relay via NIP-42, and act with the agent's relay membership and NIP-OA owner delegation.

claim: NIP-09 deletion authorization resolves the target event's author with `effective_message_author`, which — for any event signed by the relay's own key — walks the tags and returns the first `p` tag value as the "author" (crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs:768-778). That helper exists to re-attribute relay-proxied workflow messages, but it is applied indiscriminately, so it also re-attributes relay-authored *records about* a user to that user. The result is that the subject named in a relay-signed event's first `p` tag is treated as its author and may delete it with a kind:5. Relay-signed events that carry a subject `p` tag include the NIP-IA archival/unarchival deltas kind:8002/8003 (`Tag::parse(["p", target_pubkey_hex])` at side_effects.rs:3264), the NIP-43 membership deltas kind:8000/8001 (side_effects.rs:2998), and DM discovery events kind:39000 (side_effects.rs:1079). Nothing downstream re-checks: `handle_standard_deletion_event` (side_effects.rs:2253) soft-deletes the row by id once validation passes.
failure_scenario: A community admin archives a spammer's identity X (the `ConsentPath::Admin` branch, handlers/identity_archive.rs:245 — no consent from X required). The relay signs and stores a public kind:8002 delta whose tags begin `["-"], ["p", X], ["consent", "admin", <admin>], ["e", <request id>]`. kind:8002 is not in `P_GATED_KINDS` and not `is_relay_only_kind`, so it is world-readable and is the record clients follow to learn the key is retired. X — still authenticated, not banned, so the ingest restriction gate at handlers/ingest.rs:1998 passes — publishes a kind:5 with `["e", <8002 event id>]`. In `validate_standard_deletion_event`, `actor_bytes` is X (side_effects.rs:230) and `target_author` is computed by `effective_message_author` on the relay-signed 8002 event: `event.pubkey == relay_pubkey` is true, there is no `actor` tag, so the loop returns the first `p` tag — X. The equality at side_effects.rs:267 holds, validation returns Ok, and `handle_standard_deletion_event` soft-deletes the relay's own archival announcement. The relay's key never signed a deletion and the admin was never consulted. The same mechanism lets either participant of a DM delete the relay-signed kind:39000 discovery event that makes the thread resolvable for *both* parties, and lets a removed member delete the kind:8001 record of their removal.
evidence: effective_message_author(&target_event.event, &state.relay_keypair.public_key());

claim: Three of the seven RateLimitConfig knobs — agent_standard_api_calls_per_min, agent_elevated_messages_per_min, agent_platform_messages_per_min — are parsed from environment variables and documented in .env.example but are never read by any consumer, so setting them silently does nothing and agents are throttled at the human HTTP budget.
failure_scenario: An operator sees BUZZ_RATE_LIMIT_AGENT_STANDARD_API_CALLS_PER_MIN=600 in .env.example:68 and sets it to raise their agents' HTTP quota. config.rs:320-322 parses it into the struct, and then nothing consumes the field: a workspace-wide search for `agent_standard_api_calls_per_min`, `agent_elevated_messages_per_min`, and `agent_platform_messages_per_min` finds hits only in this file, crates/buzz-relay/src/config.rs, and .env.example. The HTTP bridge's only quota lookup is `state.auth.config().rate_limits.human_api_calls_per_min` (api/bridge.rs:29), applied to every principal regardless of whether it is an agent, so buzz-acp agents — which hammer POST /query and POST /count through RestClient::bridge_post (relay.rs:368) with up to 4 attempts per logical call (relay.rs:326-327) — are capped at the human default of 300/min instead of the advertised agent value of 600/min, and no amount of configuration changes that. Only agent_standard_messages_per_min is honored, at connection.rs:634 for the WebSocket EVENT path.

claim: A malformed BUZZ_AUTH_TAG is discarded silently by `.ok()` with no log line, so the agent connects with no NIP-OA owner attestation and fails membership on a closed relay with a message that names the wrong cause and is classified as a permanent rejection.
failure_scenario: An operator provisions an agent with a truncated or mis-escaped BUZZ_AUTH_TAG (a hand-edited systemd unit, a shell that ate a quote, a truncated env-file line). lib.rs:1339 calls buzz_sdk::nip_oa::parse_auth_tag(&s).ok(), throwing the parse error away without a warn! — note the sibling reader resolve_agent_owner at lib.rs:134-136 does log its verify_auth_tag failure, so the omission here is inconsistent within the same file. relay_auth_tag becomes None, HarnessRelay::connect (lib.rs:1342) sends a bare AUTH with no `auth` tag (relay.rs:3469), and on a relay with require_relay_membership the NIP-OA delegation fallback has nothing to work with: handlers/auth.rs:217 enforce_relay_membership denies, and the agent is told "restricted: not a relay member" (handlers/auth.rs:234). Because that string is classified terminal (relay.rs:3786), the agent exits immediately. The operator's entire diagnostic trail is a relay-side message saying the agent is not a member — pointing them at the relay membership table, which is correctly configured — with nothing anywhere indicating that the attestation string they supplied failed to parse. The same tag is also forwarded verbatim to MCP subprocesses at lib.rs:4211-4215 without validation, so the broken value propagates.

claim: The NIP-42 URL normalizer collapses `localhost` and `::1` into `127.0.0.1`, while its NIP-98 sibling in the same crate deliberately does not and documents that collapsing them is a host-binding side door — so the WebSocket AUTH path accepts a `relay` tag signed for a host that is a different community than the one the connection is bound to.
failure_scenario: The community registry keys on buzz_core::tenant::normalize_host, which lowercases, strips default ports and a trailing dot but does NOT alias loopback spellings — so `localhost:3100` and `127.0.0.1:3100` are two distinct communities. handlers/auth.rs:80 builds the expected NIP-42 relay URL as `ws://{tenant.host()}` (api/bridge.rs:225-231), and verify_nip42_event compares it to the event's `relay` tag through normalize_relay_url, which rewrites both sides' loopback host to 127.0.0.1 (nip42.rs:25-29). An AUTH event whose `relay` tag says `ws://localhost:3100` therefore passes on a connection bound to community `127.0.0.1:3100`, defeating the per-tenant host binding that api/bridge.rs:208-217 says the helper exists to enforce. The NIP-98 verifier states the opposite rule in a 7-line comment (nip98.rs:138-144: "No loopback aliasing ... a host-binding side door") and pins it with the test `loopback_aliases_are_distinct_hosts` (nip98.rs:289). The two sibling verifiers in the same crate therefore answer the same host-binding question in opposite directions; whichever is right, one of them is wrong. This is reachable in exactly the multi-tenant dev/test topology the media tests already model (`127.0.0.1:3100` vs `127.0.0.1:3200`, crates/buzz-media/src/auth.rs:495-499); it is not reachable as a plain token replay, because the per-connection random challenge (nip42.rs:38) still has to match, so I rate it medium rather than high.

claim: validate_video_file guards the divisor (timescale==0) before calling mp4::Mp4Track::duration(), but not the dividend. The mp4 crate computes `self.trak.mdia.mdhd.duration * 1_000_000 / timescale` (mp4-0.14.0/src/track.rs:207-210) on a u64 mdhd.duration read verbatim from the attacker's file (mdhd version 1 reads a full u64). Any mdhd.duration above 2^64/10^6 (~1.8e13) overflows the multiply before the division ever happens.
failure_scenario: Attacker PUTs /upload with a structurally valid fast-start H.264 MP4 whose mdia/mdhd box is version 1 with duration=0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF and timescale=1000. Entry: buzz-relay/src/api/media.rs:305 upload_blob -> should_stream_as_video (media.rs:49-52, matches the ftyp) -> buzz-media/src/upload.rs:292 process_video_upload -> upload.rs:421 spawn_blocking(validate_video_file) -> validation.rs:293/352. The box shape passes check_moov_before_mdat and validate_mp4_metadata_free (mdhd is in the ALLOWED list at validation.rs:859). In any profile with overflow-checks on (the default dev/test profile; the workspace Cargo.toml sets none) the multiply panics inside spawn_blocking, the JoinError maps to MediaError::Internal (upload.rs:423) and the client gets a 500 with a panic in the logs — a free crash-the-task primitive, repeatable. In release (overflow-checks off) it wraps silently to an arbitrary value, so duration_secs can land under the 600.0 cap at validation.rs:357 and be written into the sidecar as duration_secs (upload.rs:478) and returned as BlobDescriptor.duration — a fabricated duration that buzz-relay/src/handlers/imeta.rs:270 then enforces against the poster's own imeta tag.

claim: Any href that is not a recognized `buzz://message?...` deep link (including arbitrary custom URI schemes, `file://`, or other `buzz://` sub-paths crafted by a relay-controlled message author) falls through to `openExternal`, which is wired to the OS URL opener (`openUrl`) with no scheme allow-list.
failure_scenario: An attacker posts a message/link-card with an href like `file:///C:/Users/victim/secrets.txt`, a registered custom protocol handler for another installed app, or a Windows `ms-*:`/`search-ms:` URI. When the victim clicks the rendered link or link-edit card, `openPopoverLink`/`useLinkEditor.tsx`'s `openCardUrl` hands the raw string straight to `openUrl(url)` with no scheme check, letting attacker-supplied Nostr content trigger local file access or an arbitrary installed protocol handler.

claim: reader_authorized_for_event() — documented as closing the 'kindless ids:[…] lookup' read-authorization bypass for every relay delivery surface (WS historical pull, HTTP bridge, live fan-out) — only actually gates KIND_DM_VISIBILITY and KIND_AGENT_TURN_METRIC (RESULT_GATED_KINDS). kind.rs separately defines a broader P_GATED_KINDS set (KIND_AGENT_OBSERVER_FRAME, KIND_MEMBER_ADDED_NOTIFICATION, KIND_MEMBER_REMOVED_NOTIFICATION, KIND_GIFT_WRAP, plus the two above) documented as needing #p-bound read access. If any caller relies on reader_authorized_for_event as the last-line defense against the kindless-ids bypass — as its own doc comment implies — gift-wrap DMs (kind:1059), agent observer frames (kind:24200), and member add/remove notifications (kind:44100/44101) are not covered by this specific result-level gate.
failure_scenario: A relay client sends a REQ filter {"ids":["<known event id of another user's gift-wrapped DM or observer frame>"]} with no kind/#p constraint. If the read path calls reader_authorized_for_event() as its sole per-event gate rather than re-deriving the filter-layer #p rule for P_GATED_KINDS, the event is returned to a reader not in its #p tag, leaking DM/telemetry content to a non-owner.

claim: Gossip records applied via apply_gossip_record (and the underlying GossipState::apply_delta in gossip.rs) are keyed only by an unauthenticated runtime_id field inside the record with last-version-wins semantics, unlike ReadyRecord which is bound to its runtime_id by a relay-key Schnorr signature. Any peer already admitted to the mesh can gossip a GossipRecord claiming to be a different runtime_id with an inflated version number and attacker-chosen endpoint_addrs, and every peer that receives it will silently overwrite that runtime's membership entry.

claim: `write_ndjson` mirrors every outbound JSON-RPC frame verbatim onto the observer bus as an `acp_write` event, with no redaction of any field. Because the `session/new` frame embeds the agent's `nsec` (lib.rs:4198-4205), the observer payload contains the private key. claim: A relay event's `created_at` is taken raw as the channel's "latest observed" timestamp and is later folded into the published NIP-RS read marker with `Math.max` and no upper clamp against wall-clock time (`resolveChannelReadMarker`, line 114). LOW confidence on exploitability: I found a ±900s drift guard in crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs (`MAX_TIMESTAMP_DRIFT_SECS`), so a conforming relay blocks the input. This is a defense-in-depth gap — the client trusts the relay's clock check with no clamp of its own, and any relay bug, misconfigured/older relay, or clock-skewed deployment silently and irreversibly silences a channel.

Alice's client records it via `handleChannelMessage` (line 421-423) into `latestByChannelRef`. The relay-side `authors` filter constrains who may author the events, but nothing constrains what a `p` tag may name, and `query_relay` performs no signature verification. Mallory publishes a kind:20001 event authored by herself with tags `[["p", "<alice hex>"]]` and content `"offline"`. The relay returns it (it matches `authors`), and lines 363-374 assign `pk = alice` rather than `mallory`. Impact is limited to presence-state spoofing, not access control, hence low severity — but it is a concrete case of a relay-supplied tag overriding the one field the relay filter actually authenticated.

Every caller that uses `filters_match` for live delivery — `subscription.rs:450` via `push_match`, and `push_runtime.rs:244` for push-notification matching — therefore treats a NIP-50 `search` constraint as absent and matches events that do not contain the search term.

The historical portion is answered by Postgres FTS and correctly returns only matching rows, but every subsequent live message in that channel is fanned out on the same subscription id regardless of content, because `filter_match_one` ignores the term. failure_scenario: Repository OIDs are not assumed to be SHA-1 elsewhere in the codebase: crates/buzz-relay/src/api/git/manifest_event.rs:291 has an explicit test named accepts_sha1_and_sha256_oids pinning that a 64-hex OID is accepted. The pre-receive hook shares the same assumption (crates/buzz-relay/src/api/git/hook.rs:41 defines ZERO as 40 zeros, and only sets IS_ANCESTOR when both OIDs differ from that literal). The module docs state protection rules 'apply to everyone (including the owner)', so this is a protection bypass, not just a misclassification. Low confidence because I did not confirm the deployment actually provisions SHA-256 repositories — if only SHA-1 repos exist, the bug is unreachable.

claim: The streaming video pipeline creates a NamedTempFile (upload.rs:302), immediately discards the securely-created handle in favour of its path (upload.rs:303), and then re-opens that path with tokio::fs::File::create. tempfile's own documentation calls out re-opening a NamedTempFile by path as the insecure pattern and directs callers to reopen()/as_file() instead, because the O_EXCL guarantee of the original creation is lost at the moment the path is resolved a second time. File::create follows symlinks and truncates, so whatever the path resolves to at that instant is what up to max_video_bytes of attacker-supplied stream data is written into. The safe form here is to keep writing through the handle NamedTempFile already owns.
failure_scenario: On a host where the temp directory is shared and world-writable (a bare-metal or non-containerised relay with a conventional /tmp, or any deployment where another local account or a co-tenant process runs), a local attacker races the window between NamedTempFile::new() at upload.rs:302 and File::create(&tmp_path) at upload.rs:342: unlink the freshly created temp file and drop a symlink at the same name pointing at a file the relay's uid can write (a config file, a log the relay rotates, a unit file). The next video upload's body is then written through the symlink, letting an unprivileged local user use the relay as a write primitive with fully attacker-chosen content. I could not reach this from a purely remote position — it requires local write access to the relay's temp directory, so treat the reachability as unproven; the code-level deviation from tempfile's documented safe usage is what is certain.

claim: The WebSocket REQ handler runs the three sensitive-kind filter gates — `p_gated_filters_authorized`, `engram_filters_authorized`, `author_only_filters_authorized` — only when `channel_id.is_none()`. The two sibling read surfaces run them unconditionally: `handle_count` (handlers/count.rs:56-76) and the HTTP bridge `query_events_authed` (api/bridge.rs:985-1002). The comment above justifies the skip with the `fan_out()` invariant, which covers *live* delivery only; the historical-delivery branch below is a plain DB read, and its per-event backstop `event_visible_to_reader` (req.rs:387) covers AUTHOR_ONLY, SHARED_GATED and RESULT_GATED kinds but not the rest of `P_GATED_KINDS` — `KIND_GIFT_WRAP`, `KIND_MEMBER_ADDED_NOTIFICATION`, `KIND_MEMBER_REMOVED_NOTIFICATION` have no per-event gate at all (buzz-core/src/filter.rs:23-27 returns `true` for every kind except 30622/44200). I traced this and it is NOT currently exploitable: gift wraps are forced to `channel_id = None` at handlers/ingest.rs:2046-2047 (`} else if is_gift_wrap { None }`), membership notifications are inserted with `None` at handlers/side_effects.rs:942, and `EventQuery.channel_id = Some(ch)` compiles to `AND channel_id = $n` which excludes NULL rows (buzz-db/src/event.rs:400-404). The gate is therefore load-bearing on an invariant asserted three files away, not on anything local. Reporting at LOW confidence per instruction: I could not reach a failure today.
failure_scenario: Latent, not currently reachable. If any P_GATED kind ever becomes channel-scoped — e.g. someone removes the `is_gift_wrap => None` arm at ingest.rs:2046, or changes `emit_membership_notification` to pass `Some(channel_id)` instead of `None` at side_effects.rs:942 — then any member of that channel could issue `["REQ","x",{"kinds":[1059],"#h":["<channel they are in>"]}]`, the p-gated gate at line 181 would be skipped because `channel_id` is `Some`, the DB query would return other members' gift wraps, `event_visible_to_reader` would pass them (kind 1059 is neither author-only, shared-gated, nor result-gated), and the relay would deliver every recipient `#p` tag and timestamp — exactly the metadata `P_GATED_KINDS` exists to withhold. The same change made against COUNT or the HTTP bridge would be caught, because those two run the gate unconditionally.
